body.heading: Chairs, blankets, and a low ceiling
paragraphs: A good den needs a roof more than it needs walls. Drape blankets or sheets over chairs, a clothes airer, or a table, and weigh the edges down with books or cushions. A torch or a string of battery lights inside turns it from a pile of bedding into a place.
Let children lead the design. Adults are useful as engineers — holding, tying, fetching — but the den works best when the small architects make the decisions, including the odd ones.

body.heading: Give the den a purpose
paragraphs: A den with a purpose lasts longer: a reading cave with cushions and a stack of books, a café serving pretend tea, a vet surgery for stuffed animals, a spaceship with a cardboard control panel. The purpose gives everyone a role once the building is done.
Agree the end before you start if the den takes over a shared room: it stays up until bedtime, or until lunch. A clear finish avoids the late-afternoon negotiation.

body.heading: The tidy-up is part of it
paragraphs: Folding the blankets and putting the chairs back is the final stage of the expedition, not a punishment after it. Crews pack up camp together. Put the den kit — pegs, torches, a few blankets — back in one box so the next rainy day starts faster.
Photograph the best dens before they come down. A den album is a surprisingly treasured document, and it gives the next rainy day a standard to beat.

description: Blankets over chairs, a torch, and a purpose: building an indoor den is a rainy-day project the whole family can join.
